key_bets: Energy confinement time scales as τₑ ~ R² in a D-He3 dipole at meter-scale radius, yielding Q > 1 at orbital-accessible plasma conditions
D-D side reactions self-breed He3 via tritium decay at a rate sufficient to sustain commercial fuel supply without external procurement
End-to-end power beaming efficiency (proton deceleration → DC → microwave transmitter → atmosphere → rectenna → AC) exceeds ~30% at multi-MW scale
Direct conversion of 14.7 MeV D-He3 protons can achieve fusion-relevant efficiency despite ~1.4 mm proton range exceeding original Venetian blind DEC electrode gaps
A complete fusion reactor spacecraft (HTS coil, heating, conversion, beaming hardware) can be packaged within Falcon 9 mass and volume constraints
Space-qualified HTS coil with on-board cryocooler can sustain ~20–30 K operation in LEO under Van Allen radiation for multi-year orbital lifetime
Removing the vacuum vessel, blanket, and thermal cycle relocates rather than eliminates fusion plant cost, and the relocated costs (launch + spacecraft + beaming) are lower
eliminated_costs: First wall, blanket, shielding, and vacuum vessel (CAS 21–23) — orbital deployment uses space vacuum and aneutronic fuel eliminates 14 MeV neutron flux
Thermal conversion cycle: turbine plant, steam systems, heat rejection, electric plant (CAS 24–26) — replaced by direct conversion + power beaming
Tritium breeding infrastructure: Li-6 enrichment, FLiBe/Li-metal handling, tritium processing — D-He3 fuel cycle requires no breeding blanket
Neutron shielding materials supply chain: tungsten, WC cermet, boron carbide — DD neutrons radiate into space
Site, building, and conventional plant construction — no terrestrial reactor building required
novel_costs: Launch cost to LEO (~$2,700/kg Falcon 9) per spacecraft, replacing terrestrial construction CAPEX
Power beaming ground infrastructure: phased-array rectenna fields, grid tie (~$2M/MW at GW-scale SPS analogue)
Phased-array microwave transmitter fabrication (~$20M, ~25–30% of spacecraft hardware cost) — most novel hardware item, no precedent at MW-fusion scale
Direct energy converter for 14.7 MeV protons — no commercial supply chain, first-of-kind manufacturing
Orbital O&M: debris mitigation, radiation hardening, replacement logistics with no crewed-EVA precedent
He3 fuel procurement at $28–34M/kg market price, or self-breeding infrastructure if internal supply is pursued

risks.description: He3 fuel supply: market purchase at ~$30M/kg drives fuel cost to ~$1,446/MWh alone; self-breeding is categorically insufficient (~7.5% of consumption) at equimolar D:He3 and requires 13:1 D-rich ratio that destroys the aneutronic advantage

Energy conversion pathway completely undefined — Zephyr has disclosed no direct converter design, beaming technology, or ground receiving infrastructure, leaving the revenue side of LCOE formally undefined

End-to-end beaming efficiency under realistic phased-array steering is ~7–9%, far below the ~30–40% threshold required for SPS or terrestrial parity; phased-array transmitter is the dominant bottleneck (4–6 dB phase shifter loss per element)
Energy confinement scaling law for dipole geometry does not exist in published literature; D-He3 requires ~10× higher triple product than D-T, which has itself never been demonstrated in a dipole
D-He3 fusion conditions (50–100 keV ion temperature) are 2–3 orders of magnitude beyond LDX/RT-1 demonstrated parameters — TRL 1 for the foundational physics

Direct conversion of 14.7 MeV protons in any practical DEC configuration is a truly-unknown quantity; 1970s Venetian blind DEC at 50–65% used non-fusion ions and electrode gaps incompatible with the 14.7 MeV proton range

He3 procurement faces regulatory barriers independent of physical scarcity — dual-use export controls, government allocation system rationing since 2009, prioritization of national security uses over commercial users
Heating method, heating power, and recirculating power fraction undisclosed — high recirculating fraction could render the concept non-viable independent of plasma performance
Spacecraft FOAK fabrication cost (~$50–70M baseline) could be 10–100× higher; sweep shows SPS parity is lost between 1.0× and 2.0× baseline hardware cost in the optimistic scenario
Orbital HTS coil radiation hardening, cryocooler design, and lifetime in Van Allen belt environment are unvalidated at fusion-relevant field strengths
Cost framework for orbital fusion plant has no published analogue; CAS 20–60 categories largely do not apply, and the appropriate replacement structure has not been defined
Zephyr is pre-prototype, ~2 employees, with no technical papers, patents, or DOE/ARPA-E grants — entire technical disclosure fits within a single YC launch page
Orbital operations cost categories (debris mitigation, replacement logistics, orbital lifetime management) have no precedent in fusion LCOE literature
Regulatory framework for nuclear material in orbit (IAEA Outer Space Nuclear Safety Guidelines, UN COPUOS) introduces approval risk independent of technology development
